Reference

Here are some links to articles, etc. that discuss current thinking about UX and website design, grouped by concept:

"The Fold"

  • http://contentmarketinginstitute.com/2014/07/online-content-leave-above-fold-behind/
    • Also makes some good points about the (lack of) usability of the "hamburger" icon.
  • http://www.confluentforms.com/2015/01/above-fold-below-fold-attention-span.html 
    • This one refers to a jQuery library that enables you to trigger a function, or in this case push a Google Analytics event, when an element reaches a position on the screen.
  • http://www.nngroup.com/articles/page-fold-manifesto/
    •  Even though it advocates for the concept of the fold, it acknowledges that responsive design and platform proliferation makes it less relevant.

"Hamburger Menu"

  • http://moovweb.com/blog/hamburger-menu-handy-tool-or-useless-icon/
    • This showed some interesting data based on adding "menu" to a hamburger icon to increase engagement.

Image Carousels

  • http://www.velir.com/blog/index.php/2014/04/18/why-you-shouldnt-use-a-carousel-to-feature-content/
    • "Carousels can be helpful for browsing linear content where a user knows what’s coming up next – e.g. a weather application that shows the forecast for the next few days"
  • http://www.usefulusability.com/kill-conversion-killing-carousels-now/
    • "Feature one item at a time in each space. Invest the time to change your featured items often."

Eye-tracking Studies

  • http://www.nngroup.com/articles/f-shaped-pattern-reading-web-content/
    • This report is from 2006 but seems to be referred to a lot in even current articles about reading patterns on the web
  • http://www.quicksprout.com/2014/04/16/8-powerful-takeaways-from-eye-tracking-studies/
    • I found the point about using images of people to be interesting and think that might be an approach we can take with the library site to increase engagement

Resource Lists

  • https://medium.com/swlh/my-ux-reading-list-2015-b048be1a74fa#.ym8szklbs
    • Called "My UX Reading List"  has a substantial list of links to books (Amazon) that the author thinks are useful to designers, usability professionals, etc.
  • https://medium.com/salesforce-ux/7-things-every-designer-needs-to-know-about-accessibility-64f105f0881b#.9fqhn3d75
    • A useful list of accessibility tips for WCAG2.0 and Section 508

Testing Methodologies

  • http://venturebeat.com/2016/02/08/why-most-ab-tests-give-you-bullshit-results
    • "Jobr essentially rebuilt its onboarding process, informed by data on where users dropped out of the previous process."  Perhaps we can look at where visitors give up and just "google it."

 

Reference Summit 2019

(not sure who wrote this but beth is posting) Rima wrote this:)

May 31, 2019  

I (Rima Reves) attended the Reference Summit held right here on campus, in the lovely CH2MHill Conference Center. I thought it may serve me well, considering we are likely moving to a shared desk sometime soon.  

  1. We started out with a group activity where we broke into groups and talked about our ideal reference desk. The following are some of the ideas my group discussed.
    • hover board librarian: there would be no desk and the librarian/reference desk staff would go to where the patrons are.
    • Bluelight: the patron pushes a button or light and the staff person comes to them
    • Rhoomba chat:a rhoomba like item that roams the library looking for patrons in need 
    • geek squad/pro squad
    • holographic projector wherever the patron is
  2. And Now for Something Completely Different: A Revolutionary Alternative to the Reference Desk
    • Fun presentation, however it is not completely different for us as it is almost identical to what we have in the Valley Library. It turns out I forgot that Beth and Uta visited WWU prior to creating our studio. It was interesting to hear a lot of the theory surrounding the decision to go to a studio model.
    • Inquiry question and what other questions does it reuse/questioning the question/scaffolding learning/use inquiry and practice leaving
    • roving
    • flattens heirarchy that encourages participation
    • reference interview similar to inquiry
  3. The Art of the Referral: Strategies for Connecting People to the Information They Need
    • This was interesting, however,it ended up being almost exclusively about 211 info, which is a wonderful resource for community members as well as reference folks.
    • Geared towards people that are closer to the poverty level
    • There are 211 info services all around the country
      • 211 - Public, health, and community services. www.win211.org
      • 311 - Non-emergency police, fire and municipal business. Local and municipal governments will administer 311 calls.
      • 511 - Road and traffic conditions. The Department of Transportation or designated local departments of transportation will administer 511 calls in most cases. www.wsdot.wa.gov/traffic/511/
      • 711 - Telecommunications Relay Service (TRS) for the speech and hearing impaired.
      • 811 - Call before you dig number arranges for utilities to be located and marked. www.callbeforeyoudig.org
      • 911 - Emergency response. www.emd.wa.gov/e911/e911_index.shtml
    • The top ten service requests for April and May 
      • 1. Rent Payment Assistance (2,748)
      • 2. Electric Service Payment Assistance (2,019)
      • 3. Food Pantries (979)
      • 4. Housing Search Assistance (555)
      • 5. Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers (534)
      • 6. Low Cost Home Rental Listings (464)
      • 7. Low Income/Subsidized Private Rental Housing (462)
      • 8. Diapers (393)
      • 9. Food Stamps/SNAP (309)
      • 10. Community Shelters (307)
  1. Dominate Any Database in 5 Minutes or Less  
    • This was the presentation that convinced me to attend the workshop and I am glad I did.
      • She said if we only walk away with one piece of advice, it is to "READ THE WHOLE SCREEN"
      • Look for these important features,known as HALT
        • Help
        • Advanced Search
        • Limiters
        • Terms (Knowing the language and your search options will be helpful)
    • Someone brought up the fact that google has a google scholar search engine
  2. Lightening Talks
    • Census 2020
      • During the last census, we were told that if we had 40,000 more people, we would have gained another representative: https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Oregon_after_the_2010_census
      • Encouraged to encourage folks to respond to the census, so we can be accurately represented in Oregon

Replacing a Missing or Damaged Barcode

Barcodes wear with use and time and sometimes even fall off completely. For items that are stored behind the Borrowing & Information Desk (mostly equipment and keycards), we can remove the old barcode and replace it with a new one. Replacement barcodes are kept on top of the credenza between the service desks and the hold/course reserves shelves.

  • Find the item record in Alma.
    • Search Physical Items →Barcode

  • Click on the ellipsis and Edit Item

  • Replace old barcode with the new one and click Save
    • If you scan the new one in it will automatically save the record.


Reporting Alma System Outages

truenonefalse

Checking the system status

You can check the current system status at  status.exlibrisgroup.com. The Alliance Shared ILS group has provided really helpful instructions on using this page.

  1. Find the instances relevant to us: Alma NA01 and Primo NA00. You can filter the list to make it easier to read.
  2. Look at the Current Status column for signs of a known outage. Hover your cursor over the Current Status icon for details and updates from Ex Libris support. 
  3. The Scheduled Maintenance column may also provide insight into the situation, whether or not it was planned downtime.

Reporting weekday outages (Monday through Friday 8 AM to 5 PM)

  1. .
  2. Contact Ian Scofield at 7-6953, our Ex Libris point person in the library. Ian will report the outage using the Ex Libris Salesforce system.
  3. If you can't reach Ian, page the emergency on-call Library Technology staff by calling 7-8989 and leaving a message.

Reporting outages after hours (weekdays after 5 PM, weekends)

  1. .
  2. Contact Ex Libris emergency support team (24x7 Hub):

      1. your name
      2. name of institution
      3. contact information
      4. product (Alma or Primo) experiencing the problem
      5. description of the problem
    2. If you don't have access to email, page the 24x7 Hub support team by phoning or texting 877-445-5693.
  3. Also report the situation to Library Technology emergency support by calling 7-8989 and leaving a message.

Returns (Checking In)

We are happy to have returns handed to us an any Borrowing & Information desk!

The library also has self-service return options:

  • Outside returns slot near the main entrance (Available 24X7)
  • Borrowing & Information desk return box
  • Clear small items return bin located in the opening near the library entrance  
  • 1st floor returns slot in the Java II area

We check the returns stations on the 2nd floor continuously through the day. The 1st floor chute is cleared once a day at closing.

Check in Steps

Before returning items in Alma

  1. Carefully remove papers, sticky notes, paper clips, etc. from books.
  2. Give any damaged items to a staff member. Don't check them in!
  3. Sort out any ILL books and mark the band with a stamp or line with a highlighter. Place on the 2nd shelf of the return cart.

How to fill a returns cart

  1. Place items on the cart right-side up and oriented the same way: spines facing the same way, and barcode facing the same way.
  2. Hang a green "Items are Checked In" sign on the cart
  3. Place items on the cart in this order:
    1. Top shelf = general collection materials, organized by LC call number
    2. Middle shelf = Summit and ILL returns, in any order
    3. Bottom shelf = Stack oversized items, maps, and "special cases" - there are laminated bookmarks near the front desk to add notes
  4. Take full carts to the 3rd floor Annex/RAS
  5.  Bring an empty cart up to the Borrowing & Information Desk.

Closing Responsibilities

The 1st floor chute in the Java II area empties into a locked closet behind the TX compact shelving. It is cleared once a day as part of closing procedures.

Self Check Out Station

One self-service checkout station is located by the Circulation Desk (across from the cow statue near the avenue). The second station moved to the Guin Library in Newport in April 2015.

truenonefalse

Procedures

Checkout

  1. Swipe OSU ID or convenience card
    • Hold the card with the magnetic stripe facing you.
    • Or you can manually enter your card number by typing the 9-digit OSU ID or convenience card number.
  2. Scan item barcode.
  3. Press the "Finished" button on the screen to close patron record.

Troubleshooting

Rebooting the self-checkout station

  • after we experience a power blip or outage
  • at opening
  • after an Alma system outage
  • whenever the screen displays an indecipherable error message, fails to display the usual disembodied hand animation and welcome message, or otherwise freezes up (stuck on "Please wait" screen, for example)
  1. Retrieve the system logout barcode card from the key cabinet in the secure closet. It is labeled "Self-Check Logout."
  2. Scan the barcode to shut down the self-checkout computer.
  3. Turn off the unit by pressing the switch located on the underside of the table, on the front right side.
  4. Wait at least 30 seconds, and then turn the switch back on to restart the unit, including the computer.
  5. The self-checkout system will run through a startup process that includes audio prompts before settling on the checkout welcome screen. Confirm that the welcome screen appears.
    • If not, place an out-of-order sign on the unit and fill out the LIT problem report form with as much detail as possible.

Card swipe troubleshooting

  1. Make sure the card is oriented the right way (with magnetic strip facing forward).
  2. Try swiping the card a bit more slowly or more quickly.
  3. Try swiping the card at a Borrowing and Information Desk computer to determine if the problem is with the card's magnetic strip or the patron's Alma account.
  4. Try cleaning the card swipe unit. The cleaner packets are stored in the supplies cabinet. Follow the directions on the packet.

Error messages

Sometimes the error message is due to a problem with the patron account (expired or blocked). Invite the patron over to the Borrowing and Information Desk and bring up the account in Alma to investigate.

Reporting

  1. If you encounter other problems with the self-checkout unit, try restarting it.
  2. If restarting the unit does not solve the problem, fill out the LIT problem report form with as much detail as possible.

SSD Conference 2018 Notes - Bryan Feyerherm

First of all, Hood River is a very scenic location for a conference. Weather was hot but pleasant and the conference location was next to the Columbia River. Breakfast was excellant and plenty of time for eating a box lunch outside.

This years SSD Conference theme was "Support Staff: Shaping the Future of Libraries".

The Keynote speaker was Buzzy Nielsen, OLA President, who formerly was the director of the Gorge Public Libraries. Rural libraries are his particular passion. Mr. Nielsen spoke about the critical roles support staff serve in creating the future of libraries.

  • Before his presentation several support staff shared their experiences at the OLA Leadership Program and stressed that there are currently no one applying for scholarships for the next program next spring or summer. So if you are interested you may have a good chance for a scholarship.
    • One person spoke about how she never seemed to move up in her organization and how people she once trained were now above her. She learned that you can't just do your job, you need to be involved in improving your job skills outside your PD, like project management, committees, public speaking, creating projects, improving verbal/written communication skills, and teamwork.
  • Buzzy spoke about recent public library closures and how 4 of 5 have since reopened due to strong community support. 
  • Recognized staff who work at small libraries often have to do several different jobs and be able to multi-task and that many previous volunteers have become paid staff members.
  • It is important to recognize people's talents and to encourage their growth.

 

Session 1: Mindfulness at Work - Sara Webster, Beaverton City Library-Murray Scholls Branch

Managing stress is an increasingly important part of being effective in the workplace. Sara shared some videos about learning the practice of mindfulness and how it can help you.

  • All it takes is 10 mindful minutes | Andy Puddicombe (YouTube)
    • Former monk
    • Don't control thought, have a relaxed focused mind, balance allows thought to come and go without stress
    • We can't control everything around us but we can change how we experience what happens to us
    • Focus, calm, clarity
  • Using Mindfulness to Deal with Everyday Pressures | Regina Chow (YouTube)
    • Social worker
    • Improve the ability to stay in the present moment
    • Process thought without judgement
      • Improves how you experience stress
      • Allows you to make better decisions
      • Fosters wellness
    • The past cannot be changed, the future cannot be forced

 

  • Mindfulness Meditation - Guided 10 Minutes | The Honest Guys

 

Session 2: Oh No, My Ukulele is Overdue! - Checking Out a Library of Things - Brendan Lax (Hillsboro Public Library), Judith Guzman-Montes (Rockwood Makerspace, Portland), and Sara Webster (see above)

Fiction, books on CD...and metal detectors? The landscape of the modern library is changing all the time and collections of physical objects are becoming more common.

Presentation by 3 libraries who checkout non-traditional items and makerspaces.

Hillsboro Public Libraries - https://www.hillsboro-oregon.gov/departments/library/explore-the-collections/library-of-things

  • goal of lifelong learning and growth and better informed consumers.
  • Provide physical tools to help with learning new skills or hobbies
  • Give the opportunity to try new things, create and experience.
  • Items include bakeware, gadgets to accompany how-to-books, VHS-DVD conversion machines, popcorn and cotton candy making machines, musical instruments
  • Have a good return rate and patrons seem to care for the items they borrow
  • Some libraries have had tool collections for over 40 years
  • 450+ things and 21,000+ checkouts; 250+ games and 16,000+ checkouts
  • All items are holdable and renewable, 7 day checkout, $1/day overdue fine, $5 fee for not cleaning items
  • With games they do not count individual parts and pieces, just rely on patron to let them know.
  • When creating your program you should consider cost/staff time for acquisition and processing, storage space, how to handle things, who is responsible, volunteer help.

Beaverton City Library - https://www.beavertonlibrary.org/377/Library-of-Things

  • Used Hillsboro as a resource to create their own program
  • Surveyed staff and patrons for what to place in the collection
  • Were given $10,000 to begin program (learned that it included packaging for the items)
  • Created liability process
  • Verify all components when returned, but do not count individual board game pieces
  • Items are consistently checked out with long waiting lists
  • Collection includes air fryers and metal detectors.

Rockwood Library - https://multcolib.org/library-location/rockwood-makerspace

  • Very impressed with this program. Makerspace center for 6-12gr students and funded by the library foundation. 
  • Usage agreements are with students only, no parents needed. Teaches responsibility.
  • Rockwood has the largest concentration of youth in all of Portland
  • Provides snacks and lunches for low income students. Have to limit as many students want to bring food back to their siblings.
  • Students are encouraged to check out items, mess with things and just "geek out"
  • Open hours arranges around local school schedule and have programs like the "Crappy Robot" workshop and summer camps
  • Each students clocks in for statistics
  • Equipment available includes 3D printers, sewing machines, printers, CAD programs, ultimaker, laser cutter, power tools, and safety equipment. Will be getting a vacuum molder.
  • If students break the rules, they are asked to leave but can return the next day

Session 3: Building Relationships to Shape Behavior - Stephanie White, Multnomah County Library

Public libraries are experiencing a rise in escalated behavior. The session explored how relationship-building makes it easier for library staff to help patrons us the library successfully, and offered tips on maximizing personal safety.

  • Safety & security - who's job is it? Everyone's
  • Multnomah library is very intense in it's wide diversity of patrons including the homeless, mental problems and chemical dependance.
  • Serves 1300+ people on average each day.
  • Focus on behavioral rules that are less about punishment and more on guidance.
  • Collaboration (what does it mean)
    • Give patrons options, time & space, let them decide how they want to handle a situation
    • Ask questions & listen.
    • Be genuine - understand, develop your own communication style, be confident in what you say
    • Be empathetic & show respect without being judgemental
  • You need to want all patrons to use the library. You want all patrons to feel served.
  • Learn how to phrase your policies and not be so punitive. 
  • You can address issues incrementally - doesn't have to be an immediate action. Offer direction and options.
  • Often asks a problematic patron first "How is it going?" Always the answer is "ok" or "fine" but opens up a dialog.
  • Pre-emptive engagement - noticing that a patron is headed towards unwanted behavior. You can simply walk up to them and ask them how they are doing. Let them know you are aware of their actions and you can guide peoples future behavior.
  • You do not need to take verbal abuse or staff taking unwanted attention. You do not need to argue. Never share your personal information.
  • Collaborate with co-workers and keep them informed about a patrons needs or activity. Inform them of your needs and work together to prebrief or debrief on situations. Take notes for a record. Communicate well and be consistent and support each other. Be aware and ready to help or simply be present.
  • You can still set boundaries and still be empathetic. 
  • No sleeping in the library is allowed because we want to know everyone is ok.
  • Staff want to feel safe. You can best equip yourself to be safe by:
    • being aware
    • looking alert
    • any patron interaction can escalate so give yourself an exit. Distance = options.
    • body stance is important. Be confident but don't appear confrontational. Have an escape route.
    • know who is available to help.
    • practice different situations with co-workers.

Stats in LibCal

There are several ways to generate Spaces usage stats in LibCal. This page will outline the ways you can generate usage data and reports from a regular-user LibCal account. All of the tabs referenced here are found in the Spaces menu of LibCal.  Additional ways to generate stats from an Admin level account will be outlined in the Room Coordinator Manual.

Utilization Tab

The Utilization tab gives the user real-time occupancy data for spaces. It doesn't generate reports but it does allow the user to monitor occupancy of spaces when managing social distancing policy. It is best when seeking real-time snapshot information. From this tab, you can see:

  • Current occupancy of any space
  • Allowed and Maximum Capacity of any space
  • Available percentage of Allowed Occupancy and Maximum Occupancy of a space

Drop-down options allow you to target the information by filtering Zone and Category. Each column has totals at the bottom. Clicking on the links within the "Booking Activity" pane on the right side of the screen will bring up details about that activity as well such as length of the reservation and whether or not the patron has checked in or out.

Booking Explorer Tab

The Booking Explorer tab allows the user to search for specific bookings based on a variety of filters and download the results to a CSV file. The CSV file will have more information than what displays within LibCal, making it a very useful tool for manipulating data. From this tab you can see:

  • Booking ID
  • Space and Seat (if applicable) of reservation
  • Location, Zone and Category of reservation
  • Patron's name (if that hasn't been scrubbed yet)
  • Start and End times of reservation
  • Reservation Status, and if patrons are being checked into their reservations, if the patron has shown up.

Similar to the Utilization tab, Booking Explorer allows the user to narrow the results with filters. This tab has significantly more filters available, as seen in the photo below. Filters include:

  • Zone: Zones are based upon location. Remember that Zones can cross categories.
  • Category: Space categories are based upon how the space is used. A single category my cover multiple zones.
  • Space: A space may be bookable as a whole (such as study rooms) or a container for seats (such as the Rotunda)
  • Status: The drop-down menu gives you a variety of options. The default is to show all reservations regardless of status
  • Date range: Clicking on the filed will give you a drop-down menu of options. Alternatively, click on the calendar icon to select a specific date range.
  • Grouping: Bookings can be displayed individually or grouped by email or space.
  • Search: Searches can be done by patron email, name, booking form answers, or internal notes.

Once the filters have been determined, hit the "Go" button to generate the results. The light blue "Export" button will allow the user to export the results to a CSV file. Below is a link to a sample search that has been exported into Excel. Patron names have been removed for privacy. Click the link to download the file.

Here you can see how there is more information than displayed within LibCal. Part of this is due to how the information is broken down into separate columns allowing the user to manipulate the data at a more granular level than possible within LibCal. Had a Booking Form been associated with these reservations, there would also be a column for each answer within the booking form.

CSV file display note

When you download the CSV file, some columns will display ##### instead of data. This indicates the column is not wide enough to properly display the data. Once you expand the column width, the data will appear.

Occupancy Data Tab

The Occupancy Data tab allows the user to generate reports showing Occupancy Data over a specific period of time in a graphic format. As with other tabs, you can apply filters to your search for data. The filters for this tab include:

  • Zone
  • Category
  • Space
  • Date Range

Once you apply these filters, click the blue "Go" button. The report will show data in several categories:

  • Daily/Hourly Occupancy Distribution
  • Occupancy by Day of the Week
  • Occupancy by Hour of the Day

The data will display in tables, charts and graphs. These displays can be shared and in some cases adjusted. Anytime there is blue hypertext, it typically will allow the user to toggle between two different data sets.

Hovering over the "i" icon will give the user information about the data being displayed.

If there is a menu icon above the chart, clicking on it will bring up a list of options to display and download that particular chart.

Sharing reports from the Occupancy Data tab

Individual charts can easily be saved and shared but it is a little trickier to share the entire report. Printing the report to a PDF printer will save it in PDF format. This seems to be the simplest way to share a report from this tab. You may need to adjust some of the settings to get it to display accurately.


Storage Requests for Oregon Resident/Alumni Accounts

People who have Convenience Card accounts are unable to place requests for items in offsite storage for themselves. However, we can place a request on their account in Alma for them and it will be brought to the hold shelf for them to checkout. Most of the requests will be for journals, so unlike most holds you will want to place the hold on the item record instead of the bibliographic record. Here is one way to find the right item.

  1. Find the item in the public catalog and copy the MMS ID from the record. It is the number after alma at the end of the permalink.
  2. Search Alma by Physical items and MMS ID.
  3. This will give you a list of all of the issues on that record. Look at the Description field to find the right volume and issue.
  4. Click on the Request button.
  5. Choose Request Type: Patron Physical Item Request
  6.  Fill in the rest of the form with Requester, Note, and Pickup At. For the note put info about which vol/year/issue/etc is needed. The note will help make sure that the record selected has what the requested needs.
  7. Click Request.
  8. Tell patron that the item should be here in about 1 business day and that they will get an email letting them know when it is available.

Study Room FAQs

How do I search for an advanced reservation?

In the Booking Explorer tab, search for “LibAuth Account”. Click in the search bar and have the patron swipe their ID card.

Why does it say Check In when I’m checking out a key card in LibCal?

Because these are rooms not equipment. Just like when you go to the hotel, you check in to your room when you arrive and check out when you leave.

Help! I accidentally clicked twice and checked the patron in and out of the room.

Don’t panic. Find their reservation by clicking on the Booking Grid. Scroll to the bottom of the page and hover over the check out time. An option will pop up to edit the check out time. Change it to the reservation end time. If the key card comes back early, you can adjust the check out time again.

Why is there a gray area on a room in the booking grid?

If someone is trying to reserve a room, LibCal puts a soft hold on the room for 15 minutes. That way no one will book the room you are currently trying to book.

Why can’t I adjust the end time of the reservation to later in the day?

If you are making an immediate reservation, you cannot adjust the end time beyond the availability of the room. The default reservation time is one hour or amount of time the room is available, whichever is shorter. If the reservation defaults to less than an hour, it means that is the longest amount of time the room is available and you will not be able to make the reservation any longer.

What do the blue boxes on the grid mean?

That is the buffer time between reservations, currently set for 10 minutes. Patrons may check into the room during that buffer time if the key card is available.

The key card isn’t in the drawer. What should I do?

  • Check to make sure the room is actually available.
    • There may already be a reservation in place.
    • Someone else at the desk may be currently making a reservation for that same room. Because everyone is logged into the same account, the soft hold won’t show up for reservations being made at the desk.
  • If it is available, check the returned items for the key card.
  • If the key card isn’t there, check out copy 2. 

Do I still put "Student" for Faculty Immediate Reservations?

Yes, put student in the first name field regardless of the Patron's User Group. This just a uniform way to identify reservations made at the desk.

Will the patron get a confirmation email for Immediate Reservations?

No. Because we are using the valley library email address, we are not sending a confirmation email. If things aren't too busy and the patron really wants that email, you can enter their email address in the email address field and check the box to send them a confirmation email.

There are no rooms available right now but one opens up in 30 minutes. Can I make a reservation for the patron at the desk?

No. We encourage patrons make advanced reservations (even only 30 minutes in advance) on their own for a couple reasons.

The study room has been reserved for over 24 hours. What happened?

On the staff side, all of the booking limitations can be overridden. When making an immediate reservation, double check the start and end times and dates. For example, we don't want a reservation going from 9 am Tuesday to 12 pm Wednesday. When you are checking out the key card, clicking on the grid for the reservation should probably help catch those glitches. If you do find an error, you can fix it. Click on the reservation in the grid, scroll to the bottom of the page, click on the time hyperlink in the reservation and adjust the end time.

The reservation for the grad commons room is grey and says that it's status is mediated tentative. What should I do?

Since processing these reservations requires human intervention, it is possible (especially on the weekends) that you will see a tentative reservation for someone that hasn't been approved yet. If this happens, please check out the space to the person with the reservation request in place just like you would if it had been approved.

Charge:

The OSULP Sustainability Committee will work to embed sustainable practices into the culture of OSULP through the actions of its staff and users.. To do so we will:

  • Promote sustainability practices to library staff and users
  • Educate library staff and users on sustainability-focused practices
  • Work to increase the capacity of library staff and users to engage in waste reduction and waste diversion
  • Partner with campus sustainability units to maximize our impact externally and increase our options internally
  • identify energy-intensive practices and develop an itemized list for action and funding priorities

 

Mission:

The OSULP Sustainability Committee will educate, inspire, and engage our staff and users to embrace sustainable practices to benefit our environment, economy, and personal wellness.
